Now Gabriel the Greek, who was ruler over Melitene,
when he was hard pressed by the Emir Ibn Danishmand,
who used to come from Sebastia in the summer
and lay waste to the country
and consume the crops,
and go away in the winter,
sent to the Franks and swore to them three times
that he would give them Melitene.
And when they believed him,
King Bohemond went confidently to enter Melitene.
Now the Armenians who had held places since the days of Philaretus—
one, Kogh Vasil, that is to say 'the Thief', who held Kesoun and Ra'ban,
and the sons of Roupen, those who held places in Armenia—
since they feared
lest the Franks gain dominion over them and expel them from their places,
sent secretly to Isma'il Ibn Danishmand
that he should ambush the Franks.
And that cursed Gabriel also,
when the Frankish king arrived at Gafna, a village above Melitene,
began to deceive him,
and put him off from day to day until Ibn Danishmand arrived.
And he set ambushes before the king,
and captured him and sent him to Sebastia.
And he came and encamped against Melitene,
and waged war against it.
And Gabriel the wicked increased his evil deeds,
and without mercy plundered the citizens within.
Then two soldiers were moved with zeal,
and surrendered the city to the Turks on Wednesday, the 18th
of Elul in the year 1413
(1413 of the Greeks?).
In Arab copies, however, 1412.
its wealth:
for Ibn Danishmand gave all the possessions, except for human beings, to his troops.
For he did not let a single soul perish,
because he took the people for himself.
And he returned them to their homes,
and wheat and oxen and the rest of the necessaries he would bring from his country and give to them.
And Melitene enjoyed many good things in his days.
And he appointed over it as governor a certain man whose name was Basil,
a righteous and God-fearing man.
Now against Gabriel justice was aroused;
the Turks tortured him bitterly,
as well as the Christians,
especially as they reminded him of the murder of the holy bishop and the wronged notables.
